families.title: ni- (no-) vs nie- (some-)
families.rule: ni- words mean no- and the verb takes ne- as well: Nikto neprišiel (nobody came). nie- words mean some- and the verb stays plain: Niekto prišiel (somebody came).
families.bridge: Estonian works the same way: keegi with ei is nobody (Keegi ei helistanud ≈ Nikto nevolal), keegi alone is somebody (Keegi helistas ≈ Niekto volal).

families.title: Where to vs where
families.rule: After a verb of motion the word says where to: Kam ideš? Idem domov, idem von. With byť and other verbs of staying it says where: Kde si? Som doma, som vonku.
families.bridge: Estonian splits them the same way: kuhu / kus, koju / kodus, välja / väljas, siia / siin.

families.title: už vs ešte
families.rule: už is already, and with nie it is no longer (už nie). ešte is still, and with nie it is not yet (ešte nie).
families.bridge: Estonian: juba is už, veel is ešte (veel mitte ≈ ešte nie).

families.title: Aspect: one act, or the process
families.rule: The imperfective (robiť, písať, čítať, kupovať) is the process, a habit or the act itself; the perfective (urobiť, napísať, prečítať, kúpiť) is one act seen as finished, with a result. The English tense does not decide it.
families.bridge: Estonian shows it with the object: lugesin raamatut (partial, still going) ≈ čítal som knihu; lugesin raamatu läbi (total, finished) ≈ prečítal som knihu.
families.cue: What decided the form: a result, or a process?

probes.en: They organised the wedding in a hurry, in less than a month.

You're going to speak English fluently!

first.en: I was reading the book, or I read some of it.

contrast.note: Same book, same past tense. Čítal som is the reading going on; prečítal som is the book read through to its end.

timeline.imperfective: čítať (imperfective): a line with no end point. The reading goes on, repeats, or is the act itself.
timeline.perfective: prečítať (perfective): a line that ends at a result. The book is read through.

explain.trap: The English "read" does not say which twin. Ask whether the act is finished with a result (perfective) or going on, repeated or in general (imperfective).
points: The English tense does not decide the aspect: 'I read' (past) can be čítal som (the reading went on) or prečítal som (read through to the end).
A perfective verb has no present meaning: prečítam means I will read it through, never I am reading.
The imperfective future is budem + infinitive: budem čítať = I will be reading.

families.formsAcceptedBy: The verifier accepts every listed form of čítať, prečítať and pomáhať as its paradigm (verifier-rows-1.md, 2026-11-04, and the verifier's message on the critic's blockers). These three entries have no formsVerified flag in lexicon.json; the family records the acceptance instead.

families.title: tento (this) vs ten (that)
families.rule: tento is 'this', near the speaker; ten is 'that', or the plain 'the'. The English decides which one a sentence means.
families.bridge: Estonian uses see for both: tento presses 'this one here' (see siin), ten is the plain one (see seal).
families.cue: Is the thing near you, here (this), or not (that)?

contrast.note: The English decides it: this is tento; that (and plain 'the') is ten.

explain.trap: Slovak has no articles. ten points to a thing already known or mentioned, where English often says 'the' or 'that'; most nouns need nothing: Kniha je na stole = The book is on the table. Check the English: this is tento, that is ten.
